# core

[arc reference](../index.md) › [Products](../index.md#products) › **Product**

## Why it exists

```tagline
The starter kit every arc project moves in with: the door locks, the house rules, the alarm wiring,
and the move-in day that carries all of it over. Nothing else in arc runs without it.
```

# Start here

## In plain words

Picture a company that rents out serviced offices. Every new tenant gets the same starter kit on day
one: a front-door lock, fire-alarm wiring, a shared reception desk, the house rules pinned on the wall.
A tenant never builds their own front door. They move in and the building already works.

```panel big
**core is that starter kit for arc.** It is the one product every other product stands on. It holds four things:

- **The house rules** (`CONSTITUTION.md` and the rule files under `.claude/rules/`). Short written rules, for example never trust the browser to say how much money something costs. They outrank every plan and every prompt.
- **The tripwires** (the hooks in `.claude/hooks/`). Small scripts that fire on their own around what the AI does: at the start of a session, before a shell command, before an edit, at the end. They stop the dangerous moves before they happen.
- **The move-in machinery** (`arc-products.mjs` and `arc-settings-merge.mjs`). It copies arc into another project and keeps that project's own settings safe while doing it.
- **A few everyday tools**: `/arc-freeze`, `/arc-resume`, `/arc-toolcheck`, and two helpers, `researcher` and `log-analyzer`.

That is the whole product. Every other product lists core as something it needs. core lists nothing.
```

### Why this needs to be a product at all

If each tenant bolted on their own front door, their own alarm and their own reception, the building
would stop being one place. It would be a pile of rooms sharing a street number. Pulling the shared
wiring into one unit is what lets every other product stay thin. Each carries only what makes it
different, and all of them still live in one building that holds together.

arc was once one big build system. It was split into separately installable products, each with its own
packing list, so a project can take one slice of arc without dragging in the rest (ADR-0014).

| What you lose | What it looks like when it bites | core's answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe defaults** | One project allows a force-push, another does not, and nobody remembers which. | The same tripwires ship to every project, because every install carries core. |
| **One way to name a workstream** | Two commands quietly act on different lanes and the tracker drifts. | One resolver answers "which lane is this command about?", or asks rather than guessing. |
| **A trustworthy install** | A sync overwrites the settings a project spent weeks tuning. | The sync saves the project's own settings first and folds them back in after the copy. |

> The strictness of all this is a dial, not a wall. A project picks starter, standard or strict, and one
> setting moves every gate together (ADR-0008).

## arc words → normal words

```lede
Ordinary building-management things, wearing technical names.
```

```rosetta
product | one tenant in the building | a bundle of commands, agents and scripts with its own packing list
manifest | the packing list | the JSON file naming everything that belongs to one product
sync | move-in day | `sync-to-project.sh` copies arc into another project
registry | the tenancy log | `arc-registry.json`, written by a sync: which products, from which commit
lane | one workstream | a directory with its own single live plan
profile | the strictness dial | `starter`, `standard` or `strict`, set once, moves every gate
gate | a named house rule | one check in `arc.gates.yaml` that can block, warn or stay off
hook | a tripwire | a small script that runs on its own around a tool call or a session event
freeze | do-not-disturb tape | edits outside the named folders are refused
proposal branch | a change nobody has merged yet | a new branch holding proposed edits; it never touches your working files or main
```

## How a job flows

```lede
core's most concrete job is move-in day: getting arc into a project without breaking what is already there.
```

```flow
source: sync-to-project.sh <target project>
box: ① Pick the shape | whole suite, or a chosen list
box: ② Make the plan | a list of folders and files
box: ③ Copy, keep settings | project's own settings survive
box*: ④ Write the log | products + source commit
labels: names, plan, copied
out: no git repo | a note, not a silent skip
out: -
out: -
out+: arc-registry.json | the tenancy log
note: A chosen list always gets core added for free, so nobody ends up with half the guardrails.
caption: Figure 1 — move-in day. | The resolver only prints a plan; the copying is a dumb loop that follows it.
```

## The stages, one by one

```lede
Each stage is written twice: first in ordinary words, then what actually happens.
```

```steps
t: Decide the shape of the move
plain: Move in everything, or only the products you name. Either way core comes along, because nothing works without it.
d: The sync script takes the target folder and an optional products list. It always adds core to a chosen list.
f: `sync-to-project.sh`

t: Make the plan
plain: A small helper reads each chosen product's packing list and writes out the folders to make and the files to copy. Both copy scripts, the shell one and the PowerShell one, just follow that list.
d: The plan is a plain line-by-line text, so neither copy script ever has to read JSON itself.
f: `.claude/scripts/core/arc-products.mjs`

t: Copy, and keep the project's own settings
plain: Before the settings file is overwritten, its current contents are saved. After the copy, arc's wiring is folded back in and the project's own gate choices and permissions are kept.
d: The merge is a separate step so a consumer's own keys are never lost to a whole-file overwrite.
f: `.claude/scripts/core/arc-settings-merge.mjs`

t: Write the tenancy log
plain: One file records which products are installed and the exact commit they came from. Later checks read that file instead of guessing from what is on disk.
d: `/arc` reads it to draw the install and health table.
f: `.claude/commands/arc.md`
```

# The bigger loop

## A session, guarded start to finish

```lede
The tripwires are the other half of core. They are not one script; a small dispatcher runs each fragment in order.
```

```loop
top: 1 | session opens
top: 5 | session ends
stage: 1 · Open | branch, last commit, lane, tool health
stage: 2 · Command | forced push, wide rm, DB reset blocked
stage*: 3 · Edit | frozen folders refuse the change
stage: 4 · Deploy | tests first, then every gate
stage!: 5 · Close | log entry, snapshot for resume
labels: guard, guard, guard, wrap
back: last -> 1 | next session starts from the log and snapshot
caption: Figure 2 — one session under core's tripwires. | Each stage is a hook fragment, so a product can add one without editing the others.
```

1. When a session opens, one hook prints the current branch and last commit and names the selected lane. A second prints one line saying how many tools are ready.
2. Every shell command is scanned end to end for a forced push, a wide `rm -rf` or a database reset. A match is blocked outright.
3. If you ran `/arc-freeze`, an edit outside the folders you named is refused until `/arc-unfreeze` lifts it.
4. A deploy command runs the tests first, then the gates, and goes through only if none of them block.
5. When the session ends, a dated line goes into the session log. On a compaction, a snapshot is saved, and `/arc-resume` reads it later alongside the committed tracker.

## The house rules in plain words

```lede
The rule files are short and blunt. Each one is a habit written down once so it does not depend on anyone remembering.
```

- `api`: every public route is rate-limited and checks who is calling, on the server.
- `lanes`: `--lane <name>` is the only way to name a workstream, and only `/arc-kickoff` may create one.
- `stripe` and `supabase`: use the hosted checkout, keep Row Level Security on, and never let the service key reach the browser.
- `testing`: every bugfix starts with a failing test, and CI is the only gate.
- `security-sensitive` and `ui`: extra rigor on money and login, and a design review before a screen phase closes.

```panel warn
title: one thing core does not own
core runs the gates, but most gates' actual checks live in other products. It owns the runner, the strictness dial and the `reviews` gate, which blocks until every review the profile asks for is stamped on the exact current commit.
```

## Where core sits in arc

- **Under everything.** Every other product names core in its requires list. core names none.
- **Shared grammar.** The naming rule for process variants is written once in `variant-grammar.mjs`, so other checkers do not each carry a drifting copy.
- **In the face.** core has its own room in the face app. The chips at the top of this page name the room and the ring.

# Meta

## Glossary

```gloss
hook: a script the harness runs automatically at a fixed moment, such as before a shell command, without anyone asking for it.
Row Level Security: a database setting that decides, row by row, who may read or change data.
root-mode: how arc behaves in a repo that has no lanes, where one plan at the top is the only plan.
compaction: the AI's working memory being squeezed to make room; core saves a snapshot just before.
```

## Commands (5)

- [/arc-freeze](../commands/arc-freeze.md) — Lock edits to one or more directories -- a deterministic edit-boundary enforced by the PreToolUse hook (freeze-check.sh). The can't-forget version of gstack /freeze.
- [/arc-resume](../commands/arc-resume.md) — Reconstruct where we left off — position, health, scoreboard, risks, next action — from the committed tracker + last snapshot. Read-only: resume never writes state.
- [/arc-toolcheck](../commands/arc-toolcheck.md) — Full toolchain health report — every tool's status (ready / missing / stale) rendered as the project's smart-table artifact, with the exact fix for anything not ready, then offers to install/repair what's broken.
- [/arc-unfreeze](../commands/arc-unfreeze.md) — Remove the /arc-freeze edit-boundary.
- [/arc](../commands/arc.md) — arc orchestrator — read-only per-product install/health dashboard

## Agents (2)

- [log-analyzer](../agents/log-analyzer.md) — Diagnoses errors, stack traces and incident logs via differential diagnosis and first-error analysis, returning root cause + minimal fix + prevention. Use when debugging errors, crashes, or incidents.
- [researcher](../agents/researcher.md) — Researches a topic (competitors, libraries, APIs, tech choices) via web + codebase with source triangulation and confidence labels. Use for open-ended "go find out X" or "compare X vs Y" tasks.
